newsitem.title: UK: M&G Re buyout may boost SwissRe after U.S. setback.
newsitem.headline: M&G Re buyout may boost SwissRe after U.S. setback.

text.p: Swiss Re's acquisition of Mercantile & General Re may not make up for Swiss Re's recent setback in the United States, but it does provide a highly valued boost to its dominance in life reassurance.

The deal, the latest in the consolidation spree sweeping through the global reinsurance sector, was widely expected after Swiss Re's German arch rival Munich Re took over American Re earlier this month.
The move propelled Munich ahead of its rival in the United States -- the world's most important single reinsurance market -- and also extended the gap between them at a global level.

There were few other potential buys for Swiss which would dramatically improve its U.S. position, and some analysts predicted Swiss Re might switch focus and buy in an area sector where it could attain greater dominance.
M&G, Britain's oldest and largest reinsurance firm, became an obvious target. Reinsurance companies take on risk underwritten by insurance companies for a share of the premium income.
Britain's Prudential Insurance, 100 per cent owners of M&G, continually denied rumours it would sell and insisted it preferred the flotation option.
But when Munich Re bought American Re for three times its book value and with a consolidation spree in the reinsurance sector in full swing, the value of reinsurance companies was put at a premium.
That was borne out by the news on Tuesday that Swiss Re would buy M&G Re for around 1.75 million stg ($2.73 million) more than double the evaluations put on the company at the beginning of the year.
The acquisition of M&G Re does little to improve Swiss Re's overall position in the United States, but analysts believe the deal does have attractions of its own.

Only four years ago M&G was reeling from a series of losses, and a bid to sell the company to French reinsurer Scor failed largely because of conditions on price set by then Prudential chief executive Mick Newmarch.

But that year saw the arrival of John Engestrom from Skandia International as chief executive, and he has spearheaded a return to profitability by introducing a policy of commercial realism into M&G Re's underwriting.
He trimmed the company's U.S. exposures and emphasised its expertise in long term and life reinsurance.
A strategic rethink also concentrated the underwriting policy on pricing rather than premium income.
January last year saw a corporate restructure which ended the traditional division into life and general business in favour of units aimed at providing multi-line solutions for clients.
Within two years a 45 million stg loss had been transformed into a 132 million profit stg profit, and the company resumed a leading position in life reassurance markets.

"Now the reinsurer's prospects are much more secure, thanks to better underwriting controls, an improved management structure, and the worldwide recovery in general reinsurance rates," said a London analyst who declined to be named.

The corporate philosophy is based on what Engestrom calls a "true partnership with clients", where both parties are prepared to discuss business issues in the wider sense and share information in a way that goes far beyond the traditional client-reinsurer relationship.
"This approach now applies to more than half its clients, and its success has been admired within the industry," the analyst said.

"There is still an element of opportunistic reinsurance in the rest of the business in terms of pricing and capacity which is not generated through providing added-value services.But imaginative client-linked strategies are just the kind of thing that a company like Swiss Re would be attracted by."

The deal will reinforce Swiss Re's dominance in the global life market. It adds M&G's strong U.K. and U.S. portfolios, and also brings excellent contacts in the Far East and in the world of bancassurance, another strong interest of Swiss Re.

M&G Re's three main product lines are life, living benefits (health-related products classified as long-term business), and general reinsurance, with the bulk of premium income and profit generated by long-term business.
According to recent figures Britain accounted for 45%, the United States 14%, Canada 17%, Australia 11% and South Africa 13% of pre-tax profits, on a statutory basis.

However on an accruals basis, which many in the life insurance industry claim gives a better picture of growing business, the United States contributes 26%, Britain and Canada roughly 20% each, South Africa 18% and Australia 16%.
The group services customers in more than 100 countries worldwide and has an expanding global network of 30 offices.

All this should dovetail well with Swiss Re's existing business. And if Engestrom stays with the company under its new parents, Swiss Re will also gain a very effective and influential force in the reinsurance industry. ($1=.6415 Stg)
